title: Muse Enables U.S. Business Calls—But Only With a Paid Subscription, TechCrunch Reports
body:
Meta’s AI‑powered personal assistant, Muse, has moved beyond texting and web searches to become a voice‑enabled liaison that can place outbound calls to U.S. businesses on behalf of its users. The capability, first tested in a limited rollout last September, is now generally available—but only to subscribers of Meta’s paid “Muse Pro” tier. While the feature promises to streamline tasks such as booking appointments, confirming orders, or gathering information, the decision to lock it behind a subscription fee has sparked debate about the future of AI‑driven concierge services and the economics of premium AI features.

The new calling function lets Muse act as an intermediary in real‑time conversations with businesses ranging from restaurants and salons to utility providers. Users simply tell the assistant what they need—“call my dentist and ask if they have any openings next week”—and Muse initiates the call, presents the user’s request, and relays the response back through a chat interface. The AI handles the dialogue using natural‑language processing, attempting to understand nuances such as scheduling constraints, preferred times, and even polite phrasing. According to Meta, the system is built on the same large language model that powers Muse’s text‑based interactions, augmented with voice synthesis and speech‑to‑text modules to enable a seamless spoken experience.

Pricing for the feature is bundled into Muse’s premium subscription, which costs $9.99 per month after a 30‑day free trial. The free tier retains access to basic text queries, image generation, and web browsing, but the outbound‑call capability remains exclusive to paying members. Meta’s rationale, outlined in a developer blog, is that “real‑time voice interactions with third‑party services demand additional infrastructure, compliance, and support,” costs that the company deems unsustainable without a revenue stream. Critics argue that the move could create a two‑tiered AI ecosystem where only affluent users benefit from the most convenient, hands‑free functionalities.

Industry analysts see Muse’s expansion as part of a broader trend where tech giants are monetizing AI assistants beyond the traditional “free” model. “We’ve watched the AI assistant market evolve from a novelty to a utility, and now the next logical step is to charge for high‑touch services that directly impact users’ time and productivity,” says Priya Natarajan, a senior analyst at IDC. Competitors such as Google’s Assistant and Apple’s Siri already allow voice‑initiated calls, but they rely on the user’s own device to place the call. Muse’s approach—where the AI itself conducts the conversation—could set a new standard for autonomous digital personal assistants, provided it can navigate regulatory hurdles around consent, data privacy, and fraud prevention.

Privacy advocates have raised concerns about the implications of an AI making calls on a user’s behalf. The technology requires access to personal calendars, contact information, and potentially sensitive data shared during the call. Meta assures that all interactions are encrypted end‑to‑end and that users can review and delete call transcripts at any time. Nevertheless, the company must contend with U.S. regulations such as the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), which imposes strict rules on automated calls and requires explicit consent. Meta’s decision to limit the feature to paid subscribers may be a strategic move to ensure that users are more likely to have read and agreed to the terms governing such interactions.

Looking ahead, the success of Muse’s calling service will likely hinge on user adoption rates and the breadth of businesses willing to engage with AI‑mediated conversations. If the feature proves reliable and cost‑effective, it could encourage other platforms to introduce similar premium voice‑call capabilities, potentially reshaping how consumers interact with service providers. As AI assistants become more autonomous, the line between convenience and commodification will continue to blur, prompting both regulators and industry players to rethink the balance between accessibility, privacy, and profit.
